paragraphs:
Itself, by itself, alone—one, everlasting and single.
—PLATO—Sympos.

I regarded my friend Morella with a deep but most unusual affection. Chance brought me into her company many years ago. From our first meeting, my soul burned with fires it had never known before, but they were not the fires of Eros. Gradually I became convinced that I could neither define their strange meaning nor control their vague intensity. That conviction was bitter and tormenting to my spirit. Yet we continued to meet, and fate joined us at the altar. I never spoke of passion or thought of love. She, however, avoided society and devoted herself to me alone, making me happy. There is happiness in wonder; there is happiness in dreaming.

Morella’s learning was profound. As I hope to live, her talents were far from ordinary. Her mental powers were enormous. I recognised this and became her pupil in many things. Soon, however, I found that, perhaps because of her education in Presburg, she set before me a number of mystical works usually regarded as the worthless remains of early German literature. For reasons I could not imagine, these were her favourite and constant study. In time they became mine too, through the simple but effective influence of habit and example.

If I am not mistaken, my reason had little part in all this. Unless my memory fails me, abstract ideas did not affect my convictions. Nor, unless I am greatly mistaken, could any trace of the mysticism I read be found in my actions or my thoughts. Certain of this, I surrendered without question to my wife’s guidance and entered the complexities of her studies without fear. Then—then, as I bent over forbidden pages and felt a forbidden spirit kindling within me—Morella would place her cold hand on mine. From the ashes of a dead philosophy she would rake up a few strange, softly spoken words whose meaning burned itself into my memory. Hour after hour I would linger beside her, absorbed in the music of her voice, until its melody became tainted with terror. A shadow fell upon my soul. I grew pale and shuddered inwardly at those all-too-unearthly tones. Joy suddenly faded into horror, and the most beautiful became the most hideous, as Hinnon became Ge-Henna.

There is no need to explain the exact nature of the discussions that arose from those books and, for so long, were almost the only subject of conversation between Morella and me. Anyone learned in what might be called theological morality will readily imagine them; those without such learning would understand little of them in any case. Fichte’s wild pantheism, the Pythagoreans’ modified doctrine of rebirth, and above all Schelling’s doctrines of Identity were usually the subjects that the imaginative Morella found most beautiful. Mr. Locke, I believe, correctly defines what we call personal identity as a rational being’s remaining the same being. By a person, we mean an intelligent being capable of reason. Since consciousness always accompanies thought, it is this consciousness that makes each of us what we call ourselves. It distinguishes us from other thinking beings and gives us our personal identity. But the principle of individuality—the idea of that identity which may or may not be lost for ever at death—always interested me intensely. This was as much because of the striking agitation with which Morella spoke of its consequences as because those consequences were so puzzling and exciting.

By now, however, the mystery of my wife’s manner oppressed me like a spell. I could no longer bear the touch of her pale fingers, the low tones of her musical speech, or the light in her melancholy eyes. She knew all this, but never reproached me. She seemed to recognise my weakness or foolishness and, smiling, called it Fate. She also seemed to know some cause, unknown to me, for my gradually fading affection. But she gave me no hint of what it was. Yet she was a woman, and she wasted away day by day. In time, a crimson spot settled permanently on her cheek, and the blue veins stood out on her pale forehead. At one moment I softened with pity. In the next, I met the significant look in her eyes, and my soul sickened. I grew dizzy, like someone looking down into a dreary, bottomless abyss.

Must I say, then, that I longed with an intense, consuming desire for Morella to die? I did. But her fragile spirit clung to its house of clay for many days, many weeks, and weary months. At last my tortured nerves mastered my mind, and the delay drove me to fury. With a fiend’s heart I cursed the days, the hours, the bitter moments. They seemed to stretch longer and longer as her gentle life declined, like shadows as the day dies.

But one autumn evening, when the winds lay still in the sky, Morella called me to her bedside. A dim mist covered the earth, a warm glow lay on the waters, and amid the forest’s rich October leaves, a rainbow had surely fallen from heaven.
“This is a day of days,” she said as I approached. “Of all days, a day to live or die. It is a beautiful day for the sons of earth and life—ah, more beautiful for the daughters of heaven and death!”
I kissed her forehead, and she continued:
“I am dying, yet I will live.”
“Morella!”
“There has never been a day when you could love me. But the woman you hated in life, you will adore in death.”
“Morella!”

“I tell you again that I am dying. But within me is a pledge of the affection—ah, how little!—that you felt for me, Morella. When my spirit leaves, the child will live—your child and mine, Morella’s. But your days will be days of sorrow. Sorrow leaves the longest-lasting impression, as the cypress is the most enduring of trees. Your happy hours are over. Joy cannot be gathered twice in a lifetime, as the roses of Paestum are gathered twice a year. You will no longer play the carefree Teian poet with time. Knowing nothing of the myrtle and the vine, you will carry your shroud with you on earth, like the Muslims at Mecca.”
“Morella!” I cried. “Morella! How do you know this?” But she turned her face away on the pillow. A slight tremor passed through her limbs, and she died. I heard her voice no more.

Yet, as she had foretold, her child lived. She had given birth as she died, and the child did not breathe until the mother breathed no more. The child was a daughter. She grew strangely in body and mind and was the perfect image of the woman who had died. I loved her more passionately than I had thought it possible to love any being on earth.

Before long, however, the heaven of this pure love darkened. Gloom, horror and grief swept across it like clouds. I have said that the child grew strangely in body and intelligence. Her rapid physical growth was indeed strange. But terrible—oh, terrible—were the turbulent thoughts that crowded into my mind as I watched her mental development. How could it have been otherwise? Every day I discovered the woman’s adult powers and abilities in the child’s ideas. Lessons learned through experience came from an infant’s lips. Hour by hour, the wisdom or passions of maturity shone from her full, thoughtful eyes. When all this became plain to my horrified senses, when I could no longer hide it from my soul or cast it off from the perceptions that trembled to receive it, was it any wonder that fearful, disturbing suspicions crept into my spirit? Was it any wonder that my thoughts turned back in horror to the wild tales and thrilling theories of the buried Morella? I hid from the world’s scrutiny the being whom fate compelled me to adore. In the strict seclusion of my home, I watched with agonising anxiety over everything concerning my beloved child.

As the years passed, I gazed day after day at her holy, gentle, expressive face and studied her maturing form. Day after day I found new resemblances between the child and her mother, melancholy and dead. Hour by hour those shadows of likeness grew darker, fuller, clearer, more bewildering and more hideously terrible. I could bear that her smile resembled her mother’s, but shuddered at how perfectly it matched. I could endure that her eyes were like Morella’s, but they, too, often looked into the depths of my soul with Morella’s own intense, bewildering meaning. In the shape of her high forehead, the curls of her silky hair, the pale fingers that buried themselves in it, and the sad, musical tones of her speech—and above all, oh, above all, in the dead woman’s phrases and expressions on the lips of the living child I loved—I found food for consuming thought and horror, for a worm that would not die.

Ten years of her life passed this way, and still my daughter had no name on earth. A father’s affection usually prompted me to call her “my child” or “my love,” and the strict isolation of her days prevented all contact with anyone else. Morella’s name had died with her. I had never spoken to the daughter about her mother; it was impossible to speak. Indeed, in her short life, the child had received no impressions of the outside world except what could reach her within the narrow bounds of her seclusion. At last, in my weakened, agitated state, the ceremony of baptism seemed to offer an immediate escape from the terrors of my fate. But at the baptismal font, I hesitated over a name. Many names of wise and beautiful people crowded to my lips, from ancient and modern times, from my own and foreign lands, along with many, many lovely names of the gentle, the happy and the good. What made me disturb the memory of the buried dead? What demon urged me to utter that sound, whose very memory used to send the purple blood rushing in torrents from my temples to my heart? What fiend spoke from the depths of my soul when, among those dim aisles, in the silence of night, I whispered into the holy man’s ears the syllables—Morella? What being worse than a fiend twisted my child’s face and spread the colours of death across it? Startled by that barely audible sound, she turned her glassy eyes from earth to heaven, fell flat upon the black slabs of our family tomb, and answered, “I am here!”

Clearly—coldly, calmly, clearly—those few simple sounds fell into my ear, then rolled hissing into my brain like molten lead. Years, years may pass, but the memory of that moment—never! Indeed, I was not ignorant of the flowers and the vine, but hemlock and cypress overshadowed me night and day. I kept no account of time or place. The stars of my fate faded from heaven, and so the earth grew dark. Its figures passed me like fleeting shadows, and among them all I saw only—Morella. The winds of heaven breathed only one sound into my ears, and the ripples on the sea murmured endlessly—Morella. But she died. With my own hands I carried her to the tomb. And I laughed a long, bitter laugh when I found no trace of the first Morella in the burial vault where I laid the second.
